title: Why does nails become white past a certain length?
text: Imagine your fingernail is like a tiny, clear window. Underneath most of your nail, it's sitting right on top of your finger, which has lots of tiny, tiny red rivers (that's blood!). Because your finger is pink from these rivers, you can see that pink color through your clear nail window, so your nail looks pink too! But when your nail grows super long, it grows past where your finger is. Now there's no more pink finger underneath it, just air! And when there's nothing pink underneath, and just air, the clear window looks white, like a little cloud. It's just not attached to your pink finger anymore to show its color!

title: A litre is one cubic decimeter, however on Wikipedia I read that the original french metric system used the litre as a base unit. So was what first: the litre or the meter?
text: Imagine you want to build with LEGOs, but first, you need to know how long one LEGO brick is. The grown-ups in France wanted to measure everything super carefully, so they first looked at the whole Earth and decided how long their special measuring stick would be – that was the **meter**! It was like their super important first LEGO brick. Once they had that special meter stick, they could then make a tiny box using those meter sticks. How much water fit inside that tiny box? That's what they called a **litre**! So, they figured out the meter first, and then used it to make the litre.

title: Is it real that when you left the refrigirator door open It consumes more energy?
text: Yes, that's super real! Imagine your fridge is like a special, chilly box that works really hard to keep all its cold air tucked inside, like a cozy blanket keeping you warm. When you open the door, it's like opening a window in your house on a cold day – all the warm air from your kitchen rushes right in, and the cold air tries to sneak out! Then, the fridge has to work extra, extra hard, like running a marathon, to make more cold air and push all that warm, new air back out again so everything inside stays nice and chilly. And working extra hard means it uses more of its special 'juice' (electricity) to do its job. So, we close the door quickly to help the fridge not get so tired and use up all its energy!

title: If every cell on your body changes eventually, how are tattoos permanent?
text: Imagine your skin is like a special blanket with two parts: a very thin, top part that's always getting new threads and losing old ones, and a thicker, bottom part that stays mostly the same. When you get a tattoo, the artist puts the colorful ink *deep* into that bottom part of your blanket, not just on the top part that's always changing. Once the ink is down there, your body sends little clean-up helpers, like tiny little vacuums, to try and gobble up the ink because it's not supposed to be there. But these little vacuums get full of ink and then they get stuck right in that deep part of your skin. They can't move away, and they can't get rid of the ink, so they just sit there, holding onto the colors forever, even as the very top part of your skin blanket keeps changing and getting new threads. That's why your tattoo stays put!
